title: Reflections on Intimacy in the Heart of Conflict
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna's talk emphasizes the importance of approaching life with vulnerability and openness, particularly when it comes to conflict and communication. They acknowledge that conflict is an inherent part of human experience, but also offer a transformative approach by embracing our fears, hopes, and desires, and taking risks to connect with others in a compassionate and honest way. By letting go of narrow perspectives and biases, we can cultivate a sense of unity and cooperation, recognizing our shared humanity and interconnectedness.

sentences.text: Well, good afternoon everybody.
Thank you.
I wanted to start out really with some thank yous that I'm afraid I'm not going to be able to give any other time.
First of all, Norman, I wanted to thank you.
I probably wouldn't be sitting here today except that I heard you at a public talk back in 2005.
I was practicing with Shambhala at that time, but that's what convinced me to join this group.
So thank you for bringing me here.
Yeah.
Well, and thank you for bringing yourself here too for the past 25 years now.
And Tim, I wanted to thank you for your faith in me all these years, even when I didn't have any faith in myself, and also for showing me that that faith is really bigger than me.
It's bigger than something in myself.
And Jeff, my husband back there, thanks for all your support through this practice period and your help and your encouragement.
I know it took some patience and it also took a deep commitment to the relationship.
So thank you for that.
And my Benji, I want to thank my Benji for not only your logistical support but also your friendship and your kindness.
I know this was a new endeavor for you and I've really appreciated your diligence and going for it so wholeheartedly.
Thank you.
And now I'm gonna get to all of you.
When I was invited originally to be Shuso, I really felt like I didn't have the capacity for the job.
And in the opening ceremony, where the Shuso says the first time, "I'm not yet ready to be Shuso," I really meant it.
When Tim asked me the second time, I turned him down again, according to script, and said I only had two hands and two eyes, not ten thousand, and I really couldn't do it.
And I meant it again.

Then when he asked me the third time, I was again supposed to refuse, but he said that I had all these wonderful people surrounding me for my support, and he put his arms out like this, indicating so many people.
So I actually did have, he said, ten thousand hands and eyes.
The truth of that response left me speechless.
He was so right.
The drama became so real and I couldn't voice the third refusal.

So I want to thank all of our practitioners, those who came to TE, and those who came to the classes and to practice, and those who called and wrote and sent their well wishes, and all of you who are here today, especially our organizers, and I know all the folks who have put so much work into this.
I want to thank you all for coming forward and being those ten thousand hands and eyes.
But even knowing that I had all that support and that that was available, this talk was especially difficult for me.
I was worried.
How could I come up with enough words to fill the scheduled 40 minutes of talk time?
For the way-seeking mind talk, I had 68 years to draw from, but I had no idea how to approach today.
Early on, Tim attempted to assure me, and he said, "Just be yourself," or that the talk will take care of itself.
And in my head, I was thinking, easy for you to say.
Then I did the math.
If I speak for only 30 minutes, at the average rate of 130 words per minute, I have to come up with almost 4,000 words.
With a 12.5, that equals 4,000 divided by 632 words per page, which comes out to 6.32911392495 pages.
I was pretty sure I couldn't do that.
So I searched for inspiration and found these words from Blanche Hartman in her book, Seeds from the Boneless Life.
She describes the Shuso's role this way.
*The Shuso cleans the bathrooms or takes out the garbage as not to get a big head.
She sets an example of real engagement and develops an intimate relationship with everybody in the practice period.
The Shuso is invited to teach by giving Dharma talks.
The Shuso responds to the heart of the person and their question, not the words.
The most important thing is for Shusos to be completely authentic and to be willing to reveal their life, to be seen completely.
In order to be willing to be seen as they are, Shusos must be willing to be as they are.*
Now that caught my attention.
I heard the echo of Tim's words, "Just be yourself."
Well, now, who the hell is that?

The myself after a good night's sleep and a relaxing hot bath is not the myself who has been tossing and turning all night, or the myself who confidently cleaned the toilets this morning is not the myself who ardently wanted to run away at the opening ceremony.
This myself is very plastic and unpredictable.
I find her not very reliable.

Sometimes she is certainly trying to be someone, trying to keep it together, be confident, clear, and focused, trying to be generous, mindful, kind, have a tidy house, look and feel younger than she is, avoid sugar, remember names, remember anything, pay the bills, drive carefully, save all beings.

We have so many roles in life and so many roles that seem to conflict with one another, and when we start to identify with them, it gets hard to know just who is and where is the authentic voice that Blanche is speaking about.
I questioned for a while how to find that voice and over time discovered that authenticity came through the doors of vulnerability and exposure.
But even after Blanche's inspiring words, this whole exposure thing didn't feel very inviting, this stripping there in front of an audience.
So I talked to yet another teacher who said, like Tim, to just be truly who I am.
If I am tired and mindless, just be tired, be my tired self, she said.
She also suggested tossing my notes and preparation materials for my classes away, and just truly open up to the self that appeared in the moment.
Well, I wasn't quite ready to hang out with a noteless, memory-deficient self for eight weeks, and I did feel responsible for putting something sensible out to the sangha about conflict resolution.
I had promised that, or maybe that was just a rationalization, and I was just plain gutless.
Well, I decided I could be authentic in my gutlessness.
I was mildly relieved when I found an article in an old Psychology Today magazine.
It confirmed that I wasn't alone.
What drew me to the article was this opening quote from Mark Twain.
"There are two types of speakers," he said.
"Those who get nervous and those who are liars."
The article went on to say that public speaking is the number one fear in America.
The fear of death is ranked number two.
That's what it said.
We seem more afraid of public speaking than we are of physical demise, heights, jumping out of a plane, or dreaded in-laws.
If you think about it, this is still the article, fear of public speaking is also a fear of death, an emotional death, and I would add an ego death.
We feel naked and exposed in front of an audience.
We think people are going to scrutinize everything we say and do.
We pressure ourselves to be perfect, or else our self-worth suffers.
We dread confronting the possibility of rejection.
It sounds crazy, but the article I read was right.
Speaking did at times seem like a fear worse than death.
At first I took on a battle to beat nervousness, but knew from practice that resistance just makes the matter worse.
So as I had been taught, I just watched it: the thoughts, the body sensations, and the emotions it swam in.
And after a while, it mostly just popped up when I heard or I read the word [unclear: "hosanchiki"].
Although I enjoyed Mark Twain, Psychology Today's advice is pretty limited.
I remembered the social researcher Brene Brown and revisited her well-known TED talk on vulnerability.
She defined vulnerability as uncertainty, risk, and emotional exposure.
It comes from the Latin word vulnerare, which means to wound, to be open to attack, and capable of being hurt.
And we have to do it, she learned, if we want to open up to courage and compassion and lead lives filled with joy, gratitude, and connection.
A wholehearted life, she called it.
She goes on to say, "We are the most in debt, obese, addicted, and medicated adult cohort in U.S. history.
The problem is that you cannot selectively numb emotion.
You can't say, here's the bad stuff.
Here's vulnerability.
Here's grief.
Here's shame.
Here's fear.
Here's disappointment.
I don't want to feel these.
I'm going to have a couple of beers and a banana muffin.
You can't numb these hard feelings without numbing," and this is still Brene Brown, "you can't numb these hard feelings without numbing the other effects.
You cannot selectively numb.
So when we numb those, we numb joy, we numb gratitude, we numb happiness.
And then we are miserable.
We have a couple of beers and a banana nut muffin.
And it becomes this dangerous cycle."

Reading this two or three times, thinking of not a banana nut muffin, but maybe a bar of really dark chocolate, I started to muse on the vulnerability of my class topic, intimacy at the heart of conflict, and its relationship to authenticity and vulnerability.
The very fact of our being born into this world with our need to interpret it, separate, and mediate our experience through language means that we are in conflict.
We began with a conflict within ourselves when we first left the Garden of Eden, when we split ourselves off from our inherent Buddha nature.
The book of Genesis says that we ate the fruit of good and evil.
To me, that's the time when we split the world into two, into right and wrong, you and me, yes and no.
And Genesis continues to say that Adam and Eve covered their nakedness.
Our original nature, our truly authentic self, was covered over.
And we built up personas, put on our masks and fooled ourselves.
Our feelings are in conflict with our thoughts, our bodies in conflict with desires, our good intentions in conflict with our actions.
And more obviously, we're in conflict externally with our neighbor, our government, our environment, and even our gods.
Our great literature pivots around the theme of conflict because conflict is universal.
Sounds bleak, but it ain't necessarily so.
As I've been talking about through these weeks, there's redemptive value in this conflict.

And as I've been studying and practicing with conflict, both internally and externally, I've learned that the redemptive voice of conflict, which can transform it into intimacy, is the voice that's open to the unpredictability of the next moment.
If you attended our conflict classes, you'll remember that there's an opportunity during the rising tension of a conflict to use that energy creatively.
When we can catch what's called the balcony of our emotional cycle in a disagreement, we can convert that bodily flow of energy into insight and understanding.
It's a fleeting opportunity, completely new at every moment, at every meeting, to use all of our previous practice of presence and mindfulness.
If we miss that moment, we can fly into an emotional tailspin.
I've been studying and making use of this moment on the balcony.
For our conflict class, participants practice with an actual person in their life.
And who better to pick than the one we're most intimate with?
As Norman says in training and compassion, quote, "getting along with others is very complicated.
And the better we know others, the closer to them we are, and the more dealings we have with them, the harder it gets."
Jeff and I have been together for 37 years, and have had our dances with conflict.
So I've been practicing advancing with courage and honesty, and I've really taken a fresh view of conflict as an opportunity for a deeper way of listening and expression.
And that can be dangerous to the ego.

When we hit this balcony in a tough discussion, this pivot point of opportunity, I notice how choice emerges, how the [unclear: "marrow of myself making and masking"] competes with the bodhisattva of my authentic voice.
The voice that has to prove itself, my opinions, my competence, my need to be right, my self-image, that is not my authentic voice.
But then on pausing, I can see this balcony as a vantage point.
I look down into not only my deeper and more genuine feelings, but into my often invisible truer nature.
I can see Mara trying to protect a position, a position that in reality is only a projection or judgment born out of the past that doesn't reflect the reality of this moment.
Can I choose to act in line with my intention to break down the barriers and defensiveness, to use the tenets of right speech, to practice the art of deep listening?
Can I acknowledge and bring forward my fears and my hopes and wake up and even share that tender and wounded place in my heart?
Can I sit in the seat of the man who is across from me and feel the sorrows and aspirations that live in his heart?
On the other hand, there may be a situation where no, or setting a limit, is the appropriate response.
If this is the case, I might risk rejection or some temporary alienation.
Do I hesitate to bring myself forward to avoid the tension and keep an uneasy peace, and allow my pride to pass up an opportunity for honest self-exposure that could deepen our connection?
I'm really feeling this, you guys.
I didn't know.
Thanks, Jeff.
So I study carefully how to say a compassionate no that honors both myself and the other person.
Thank you.
And I trust [unclear: "Brunet's"] research that by taking the risk of exposure, I open up to a deeper connection and relationship between us.
Gosh, we had one practice period.
Okay, this is the exposure, I guess.
With the topic being conflict, I can't help bringing politics into the midst of our sesshin.
It's ever-present and still calls for great consternation for many of us.
I know last night when we were sitting it was so peaceful, and I thought, oh, I don't think I want to bring politics into this today.
But it was already in the talk and I didn't want to get rid of it.
But I also know, talking to people when I did [unclear: "tease"] with people, how often it came up and how very present it still really is in our minds.
So a week ago the Conservative Political Action Conference was underway.
A conference that only a few years ago banished Steve Bannon and rejected Donald Trump, but now welcomed them both with open arms.
Yet there were positive notes to this conference.
The conference condemned the alt-right and barred the hate speech of Milo Yiannopoulos, the brash former editor of Breitbart News, the newspaper of the extreme right.
What's true is that a week from today a new reversal, another alternative fact, or a shocking or contradictory statement will be made again.
And what we can take from that more than anything is that we are living in incredibly uncertain times.
And uncertainty provides [unclear: "great-father"] for practice.
I want to recall case five from the [unclear: "New Mankan"], man in a tree.
I don't know how the great Roshis interpreted this [unclear: "con"], but I see it as a metaphor for our current conditions and how vulnerable we are right now.
Jin Yiann said,
*It's like a man hanging in a tree by his teeth over a precipice.
His hands grasp no branch, his feet rest on no limb.
And at the bottom of the tree someone stands and asks him, what is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the west?
If the man in the tree does not answer, he fails in his responsibility to the person below.
And if he does answer, he falls and loses his life.
Now what shall he do?*
Many of us right now seem to be hanging onto a limb.
We are in the midst of turmoil, not only as a nation, but as mutual inhabitants of this earth.
Everything on the planet is entirely laid bare to all our human actions, whether nurturing or destructive.
We seem to be scrambling to find a way to act, to do something, anything, to turn the tide of our nation as well as of our planet.
And like the man in the tree, we feel responsible, yet dangling in an impossible and sometimes powerless position.
We watch as a small cadre of powerful individuals, twisted by conditions they or I don't understand, manipulate millions of people.
Our newly appointed leadership, bolstered by wealthy alliances and media sources, is turning the truth and exploiting and intentionally aggravating the fears and emotions of everyday people.

The president's chief strategist and influential advisor has said quite openly, and these are from quotes that I read, that we must engage people's fear, hatred, anger, and competitiveness in order to bring about his brand of ethno-nationalism.
As a cunning advisor, he uses even the president's personal insecurities and desperate need for recognition and fame to boost his agenda.
So I don't believe that November's election revealed a nation of mean-spirited and hateful citizens.
I do believe that most Americans who voted for this president in Congress did so with a decent and understandable intent.
An intent to protect themselves and their families and to find some security in what they see as a very threatening world.
Our brains crave familiarity and safety, and that makes it so easy to succumb to promises of good-paying jobs, of tightly secured borders, and protection for strongly held religious beliefs.
And no matter what side we're on, we're capable of clenching our teeth onto our narrow perspectives and biases, and of reducing the complexities of our human affairs into simple tweets and labels.
And from there, how easy it is to stick our heads in the sands of complaint or despair and avoid taking any responsibility.
We become the man in the tree, not able to respond.

Thinking about this need to grasp onto some safe branch of security, I had to examine myself and how I look at the world through my own ideologies, and imagine myself to be more broad-minded or less biased than the folks on the other side.
But how deeply have I looked at the other side?
Have I been looking as one who shares roots with every being on this planet?
I do see that I look for views that confirm my positions, as do the companions I choose to hang out with and the businesses I choose to patronize.
There are thoughtful and reasonable people who disagree with me and might give me some newer perspectives and deeper insight into the needs and fears of those I don't understand.
I don't need to agree with their opinions or excuse tactics that are harmful to others.
But wouldn't it be wonderful to have a talk with my neighbor over the fence and see how much we really have in common?
Concerns about our children, aging parents, our economic futures, and our inevitable old-age sickness and death.

So I look at my own fears that keep me clenching my teeth on that branch, and the times that I've been unwilling or unable to acknowledge that those I consider as other are also holding on to that same branch, in that same precarious and vulnerable position.
How open and patient am I to feeling and hearing their pain and seeing through their words to the desperation below?
I know that to open to their pain, I have to look into the darker shadows of my own heart.
There is another way to look at Jingyan's branch.
Hanging out on a limb of uncertainty, especially when our anxiety and fear is being manipulated, is difficult to do.
But this limb can be seen as a perch for looking out with freshness and curiosity, for maintaining our don't-know mind.

We can use it as a vantage point for living out our practice, for staying mindful of our precepts and our vows to relieve suffering, and to realize that single thread of life that permeates all things.
From that branch of inquiry and open-hearted concern, I can watch my reactive tendencies and understand when they will taint my interactions and further polarize the issue.
When I step out the door of my house and encounter my neighbor who advocates arming citizen militias, how do I meet him?
Can we speak openly about our positions, asking each other hard questions from a place of real inquiry, and still maintain some care between us?
Or do we continue to nod and wave from across the street, avoiding any close encounter?
Can I just keep dangling here and maintain my intention to meet him with compassion, yet stand solidly on the ground of my ethics and values as I am sure he feels he must do?
I do get disturbed by those who cause harm to others through their use of wealth and power, and I do get that fundamental civil rights, among others, are seriously at stake.
But really, we can't separate the victims from the perpetrators.
How can we compare suffering?
Can we extend our compassion to the immigrant waiting in fear to the customs enforcement officer, yet withhold it from a suffering president who cowers behind his gilded name on a tower?
Isn't it all suffering?
We may deny it or bury it with our blustering or lies or addictive entertainment.
But in the end, it is really all our suffering.
And it knows no boundaries of color, religion, political parties or socioeconomic status.
It's my hope that if we all hang out long enough, with enough care and curiosity, maybe we'll recognize deeply in our bodies and bones this groundless position we're all in.
It is the same position we've always been in and will continue to be in, living with the fact of our impermanence and inevitable death.
Now, I was going to stop here until just a little while ago.
But I've gone beyond my 6.32911392495 pages.
So I did think I was going to stop.
Until the other day, I had this sort of addendum kind of experience that I want to share.
I was reminded of our man in the tree [unclear: "cone"] again this week when I was absorbed in a domestic conflict.
It took place at the bird feeder.
Dangling upside down by his back feet from the limb of a cedar tree in our front yard was a portly squirrel I eventually called Jing Yan.
Below were his competitors, the blue jays going after the thrush, the thrush chasing off the juncos and the juncos after the chickadees.
No lobbying, no filibuster, no flight to Mar-a-Lago.
They simply ate all the seeds that my squirrel was spilling as he hung upside down, giving them the evil eye.
His own greed, compelling him to defend his territory, was actually feeding his competitors.
So this is what they mean by trickle-down economics.
I watched my dangling squirrel as his back leg lost its precarious footing on the limb.
In an instant, he lost his hold and tumbled and turned almost 180 degrees around before he hit the ground.
He was a little humbled and chagrined, it seemed to me, but ready to scurry right back into the activities of his daily life.
No wavering, no looking back.
So maybe that's the 180-degree turn and fall from the limb that we all have to take.
At first, we hunker down on our perch with our eyes on the enemy and we enclose ourselves with our outer identities and distractions.
But then something shocks us.
Some crisis emerges.
A birth or a death or maybe some loss or heartbreak where no resolution is possible.
There's no place to run to.
No banana, [unclear: "not muffin"].
Not even room to lash out.
We're hanging in the place between yes and no.
I'm beginning to look at the fear that is naturally a part of our life as an ally, not an enemy.
And through no act of will, we open.
We're free falling.
We just quietly watch the squabbling creatures outside the window at the cedar tree.
But now, what once looked like a battle is a perfectly balanced play of life.
And from there, like my squirrel, we pick up our responsibilities once again.
We go back to our cushions.
We open up to the play of time and change.
Our world will get entangled again and we'll return again and get hung up again in its cycle.
Yet we continue to reaffirm our vow to leave our hearts and minds wide open to every magnificent being and every magnificent storm.
We begin to realize that the really dangerous place to be is inside our constricted walls of self-concern.
And we remember that together and only together, we really do have a thousand hands and a thousand eyes.
Thank you very much.
*My intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of this way. [unclear: "Divisions"] are exhaustible.
I vow to end them. [unclear: "Bates"] are boundless.
I vow to enter them. [unclear: "Divisions"] are exhaustible.*
